text: You get an m by n matrix. Every row goes up left to right, and the first number of each row is bigger than the last number of the row above it. Tell me whether a target is in the matrix. It has to run in log of m times n time.
Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I only return true or false, not the position. Is that right?
And every row has the same length, so there are no ragged rows?
Good. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Both dimensions up to a hundred, values within about ten thousand either way.

Let me name the thing that makes this easy. Those two rules together say something stronger than they look. Rows go up, and each row starts above where the last one ended. So if I glue the rows end to end, I get one long sorted list. That means this isn't really a 2D problem. It's a 1D binary search that got folded into a rectangle.

Let me run through the example. Take the rows one, three, five, seven; ten, eleven, sixteen, twenty; and twenty-three, thirty, thirty-four, sixty, and look for three. The first numbers of the rows are one, ten, twenty-three, and that column is sorted on its own. Three sits between one and ten, so if it's anywhere, it's in row zero. Then I search that row and find it. For thirteen, the same logic points at row one; I search ten, eleven, sixteen, twenty, and it isn't there, so false.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to check every cell, which is m times n, and uses neither rule. A middle option is to walk down the rows to find the right one and then binary search it — that's m plus log n. It would pass at these sizes, but it only uses half the structure. This problem reminds me of binary search for a boundary, done twice. The column of first numbers is sorted, so I can binary search that to pick the row in log m. Then the row itself is sorted, so another log n. Added up that's log m plus log n, which is log of m times n. There's also a one-pass version that treats the whole thing as a flat array. I'll mention it at the end — same complexity.

Here's the plan. Two binary searches, same skeleton. One: search the first-number column for the first row that starts above the target, with a strict greater-than. Two: take left minus one as the row; if left is zero, return false. Three: search that row down to one cell and check it. One thing worth flagging — pass one gives me the first row that's too big, and I want the one before it, because a row starting above the target is entirely above it. Left minus one is negative one when the target is below every row, so that guard is required. The same reasoning forces the strict greater-than: with greater-or-equal, a target equal to a row's first number makes that row the boundary, and left minus one lands one row too early. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Pass one runs left from zero to m over the first numbers, keeping mid as the right bound when that row starts too high. Then the guard, then row index is left minus one. Pass two resets left to zero and right to n minus one, and converges on one cell. The return still compares that cell to the target, because converging only gives me a candidate, not a hit. One thing worth flagging — there's an asymmetry people often fix and break. I guard left equals zero, but I do not guard left equals m. Landing on m just means every row starts at or below the target, so left minus one is m minus one, a perfectly real row — and the target may well live there. A symmetric guard would throw away every answer in the bottom row.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. The matrix above, target three; I expect true. The highlighted row is where it matters: pass one stops with left at one, the first row that's too big, so the row is zero and the guard passes. Pass two converges on index one, which holds three — true. Let's also test with corner cases. Thirteen converges on sixteen in row one; the value check returns false. Zero: every row starts too high, left is zero, and the guard returns false. A hundred: left runs to m, the last row converges on sixty, and the value check returns false. A single cell or a single column returns true. Those three false cases take three different exits. I also brute-forced every matrix up to four by four against every target — two hundred eighty cases, all correct.

The time complexity is log m plus log n, which is log of m times n — about seven plus seven rounds at these limits. The space complexity is constant. Even a hit pays both passes in full — there's no early exit. Oh, one more thing — the flat version. Since gluing the rows gives one sorted list, I can binary search indices zero to m times n directly, turning an index into a cell with a divide and a mod by n. One loop, no left minus one reasoning; the trade is that arithmetic every step. I'd also flag what this leans on: each row starts above where the previous one ended. Drop that, keep only rows and columns increasing, and gluing no longer gives a sorted list. That's a different problem, usually solved by walking in from the top-right corner in m plus n.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You turned the two given rules into one sentence — glue the rows and it's sorted — and built everything from that. You explained left minus one as the last row that isn't too big and tied the strict greater-than to it, instead of arriving at the sign by trial and error. And you called out that the left guard has no right-hand twin, which is exactly the fix people add and regret. Good work.
